name: The Categorical Imperative
statement: Act only on a rule you could will everyone to follow, and treat people as ends, never merely as means.
statementAccent: treat people as ends, never merely as means
meaning: The categorical imperative is the supreme principle of morality in the ethical philosophy of Immanuel Kant, set out primarily in his 1785 Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals. It is a command that applies to all rational beings unconditionally, that is, categorically, regardless of their particular desires or goals. Kant contrasted it with hypothetical imperatives, which command only conditionally: if you want some end, then take the necessary means. A hypothetical imperative binds you only if you happen to have the relevant desire, whereas the categorical imperative binds every rational agent absolutely, simply in virtue of being rational. Kant gave several formulations that he regarded as equivalent expressions of the one principle. The Formula of Universal Law directs one to act only on a maxim, a personal rule of action, that one could at the same time will to become a universal law binding on everyone. The Formula of Humanity directs one to treat humanity, whether in oneself or in others, always as an end and never merely as a means. Further formulations invoke autonomy and a kingdom of ends. The categorical imperative is the cornerstone of Kant's deontological ethics, which grounds morality in duty and rational principle rather than in consequences, and it deeply shaped modern ideas of human dignity.
mechanism: The categorical imperative provides a test for whether an action is morally permissible, based on reason alone rather than on the outcomes an action produces. Kant held that morality must be grounded in principles that any rational being could recognize, independent of particular desires, so the moral law takes the form of an unconditional command. The Formula of Universal Law operationalizes this: before acting, one identifies the maxim, the underlying rule of one's intended action, and asks whether one could consistently will that everyone act on that same maxim as a universal law. If universalizing the maxim leads to a contradiction or something one could not rationally will, the action is forbidden; Kant's classic example is that a maxim of making false promises cannot be universalized, because if everyone did so the practice of promising would collapse. The Formula of Humanity approaches the same requirement from another angle, insisting that because rational beings have an intrinsic worth, or dignity, they must always be treated as ends in themselves and never used merely as tools for someone else's purposes. Kant considered these formulations different presentations of a single principle, all flowing from the idea that a rational will legislates moral law for itself and for a community of rational beings, a kingdom of ends. Moral worth lies in acting from duty in accordance with this law, not in the consequences.

examples.text: Kant's rule to act only on a maxim one could will to become a universal law, as when a false-promising maxim cannot be universalized.
The Formula of Humanity requires treating people always as ends in themselves and never merely as means to one's own purposes.
A hypothetical imperative binds only if you want some end, while the categorical imperative binds every rational being unconditionally.

whyItMatters: The categorical imperative is one of the most important ideas in the history of moral philosophy, providing the foundation of Kant's deontological ethics, in which the rightness of an action depends on whether it conforms to rational moral duty rather than on its consequences. By grounding morality in a principle that any rational being could recognize and will, Kant offered a powerful alternative to consequentialist theories such as utilitarianism, and his insistence that people must always be treated as ends in themselves, never merely as means, gave philosophical form to the modern idea of human dignity and equal respect. This has deeply influenced ethics, human rights, law, and moral reasoning about issues from lying and coercion to exploitation and consent. The demand that moral rules be universalizable, applicable consistently to everyone, remains a touchstone for testing moral principles, and the idea that morality flows from the autonomy of a rational will shaped later thought about freedom and moral agency. Even critics engage the categorical imperative as a central reference point.

working.text: identify the personal rule, or maxim, on which you propose to act.
ask whether you could consistently will that everyone act on that same maxim as a universal law.
ensure the action treats people, including yourself, always as ends in themselves and never merely as means.

limits: The categorical imperative is profound but faces well-known criticisms. It is charged with rigidity and absolutism, most famously in Kant's own claim, in his 1797 essay on a supposed right to lie, that lying is always wrong even to a would-be murderer asking where an intended victim is hiding, a conclusion many find morally unacceptable. The framework can also generate conflicting duties, giving limited guidance when two absolute duties collide, and it is criticized as abstract and hard to apply, since determining the relevant maxim of an action and whether it can be universalized is often contestable. Some critics argue that testing whether a maxim can be universalized smuggles consequences back in, contrary to Kant's aim, and its grounding of moral status in rational agency raises hard questions about beings who lack full rationality.
misreadings: The categorical imperative is not a rule about achieving good outcomes; it is a duty-based test that judges actions by whether their maxim can be universalized and respects persons as ends, not by their consequences. It does not mean merely being consistent about anything one wants, but willing a maxim as a universal law binding on all. And Kant's own strict applications, such as forbidding all lying, are controversial rather than obviously correct, so treating the imperative as consequentialist, as bare consistency, or as beyond the difficulties of its rigid conclusions, misreads Kant's supreme principle of morality.
origin: The supreme principle of morality in the ethics of Immanuel Kant, set out primarily in his 1785 Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, commanding rational beings unconditionally through several equivalent formulations.
